extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: A compilation of doctrinal rules and evaluative standards from a patent-law treatise covering re-issues, conception and reduction to practice, novelty, utility, abandonment, prior use, identity tests, claims (form/scope/interpretation), combinations, caveats, and related procedural doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot cover new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue cannot cover new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly cited (e.g., 668 n.10). A reissue cannot be used to add subject matter that was not described in the original patent; it cannot cover subsequent inventions or new matter introduced after the original grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception complete when idea ready for reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is complete when the idea is ready for reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception is fixed when the inventor has a definite and permanent idea of the complete invention such that one skilled in the art could reduce it to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay unreasonable if over two years
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay in acting (e.g., in seeking reissue or correction) is unreasonable if over two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreasonable delay can bar relief (e.g., reissue, disclaimer) and may be evidence of abandonment or prejudice; courts treat multi-year unexplained delay skeptically (see 690 n.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may enlarge claims (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue may enlarge claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although reissue can in some circumstances broaden the scope of claims (see multiple citations, e.g., 656), enlargement is constrained by prohibitions on introducing new matter, by delay, and by requirements that the enlargement be due to inadvertence, mistake, or accident without fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner’s jurisdiction over re-issues and finality
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction of the Commissioner over re-issues — how far conclusive; decision of Commissioner final as to fraud in re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative determinations by the Patent Office Commissioner on reissue and fraud have particular conclusive effects, though subject to judicial review in defined circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue allowable whenever defect discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue allowable whenever defect discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee who discovers a defect in the patent may seek reissue to correct it, subject to statutory and equitable limits (e.g., no new matter, no undue delay, no fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue of combination patent may cover subcombinations and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue of a combination patent may cover subcombinations and elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue of combination patents may properly claim subcombinations or individual elements in certain circumstances (see 671–672), but such claims are limited by what was originally described and by the prohibition on adding new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may cover practicable form where original impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue may cover a practicable form when the form in the original was impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original disclosure included an impracticable embodiment, reissue may be used to claim a practicable embodiment described or attempted in the original, provided no new matter is introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue construed to sustain it if possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue should be construed to sustain it if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Patent Office will attempt to interpret reissued patents so as to uphold their validity where a reasonable construction permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery an essential element of the inventive act
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery is an essential element in the inventive act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An act of invention ordinarily includes a discovery of a new principle or mode; mere mechanical skill without discovery may not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice necessary (principle & instruments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practical art or instrument is necessary; reduction to practice is generally required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For patents on many inventions, especially machinery and processes, actual reduction to practice (or constructive reduction via an adequate specification and claims) is required to establish rights; principle reduced to practice may be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence required from date of conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence in reduction to practice is required; diligence required in earliest conceiver from date of conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor must exercise reasonable diligence from conception to reduction to practice; failure to show diligence can defeat priority and support findings of abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use is not public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use is not public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of an invention for experimental purposes, testing, or development does not necessarily constitute a public use that would bar patentability, provided the use has essentially experimental character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility as evidence of novelty and inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility can serve as evidence of novelty and inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated practical utility may support findings of novelty and of inventive contribution, particularly where utility shows a new result or function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and universal novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is required; universal novelty necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention must be new (novel) over the prior art generally; universal novelty means it must not be known or used anywhere before the patent date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description construed with other parts of the specification; ambiguity in description
rubrics_metrics.description: The description is construed with other parts of the specification; ambiguity in the description is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is read as a whole; ambiguities may make sufficiency a question of fact, may render a claim void, or otherwise affect claim scope and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment by describing and not claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment may occur by describing and not claiming an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If matter is described in the specification but not claimed, that omission may be treated as abandonment to the public in some circumstances; whether omission equals abandonment depends on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay as evidence of abandonment to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay may be evidence of abandonment of the invention to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long unexplained delay in asserting rights or prosecuting claims can be evidence that the inventor has abandoned the invention to the public, affecting rights and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use avoids patent; essentials of prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior knowledge or use of the invention (prior use) avoids patent; essentials of prior use described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior public use/sale/known practice by another that anticipates the invention can defeat patentability. The treatise catalogs requisites (e.g., accessibility, identity) for prior use to be a bar; catalogues and sales can be evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity tests for machines, manufactures, compositions, and combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity of machines, substance/form, designs, combinations, and elements is a key test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various tests determine whether an accused device or prior thing is 'identical' to the patented invention (shape, proportions, arrangement, cooperative law of elements, result). Identity can be a jury question; subcombinations and equivalents also considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: purpose, requisites, and essential relation to specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims serve a particular purpose and have requisites; they are essential to the specification and define the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are the legal definition of the patentee’s monopoly; they must satisfy statutory and doctrinal requisites (clarity, support in the specification, definiteness) and must correspond to what is described so skilled artisans can practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim is in effect an independent patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim functions as an independent patent right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim stands on its own for validity and enforcement; multiple claims can exist but each must independently meet requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must be precise, complete within itself, and define the invention; ambiguity is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must precisely define the invention, be complete within itself, and ambiguity in a claim is fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must 'precisely define' the invention, show the class it belongs to, be capable of standing or falling alone, and contain no useless or equivocal language; courts construe claims as a matter of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims confined to a single and distinct invention; cannot join disparate inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be confined to a single and distinct invention and cannot cover principal and subordinate inventions together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joinder of different inventions in one claim is improper; claims should not attempt to embrace multiple distinct inventions in a single claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must include all essential features and exclude non-essential features
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must include all essential features of the invention and exclude non-essential features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid claim embraces the essential elements necessary to produce the claimed result; it must not include irrelevant matter and should exclude non-essential features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be limited to the actual patentable character of the invention; cannot claim principles, effects, or mere functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be limited to the patentable character of the invention and must not claim a principle, mode of action, idea, or mere result/effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claims that are merely statements of effect or result are void; where possible, functional language should be construed to cover the means disclosed, but a claim cannot claim all modes of achieving a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional language and 'means' claims — how construed and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims using functional language ('means', 'mechanism', 'for doing X') are treated specially: they may be construed to cover disclosed means but can be improper if they attempt to claim mere function without structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claims should, if possible, be read to cover the corresponding disclosed means; purely functional claiming of a result or all modes of performing a function is generally improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must correspond with the description and be based on sufficient description
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must correspond to the description and be for matter properly and sufficiently described so that skilled artisans could practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that attempt to cover matter not supported by the specification or that rely on insufficient disclosure are invalid; the description may aid construction but cannot enlarge an inadequate claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims control when inconsistent with the description; description cannot enlarge claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims and description conflict, claims control; description does not enlarge claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the description construes the claims, claims define the scope. A specification cannot be used to expand the claim beyond its proper meaning; contradictions may render both invalid in extreme cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must stand or fall as a whole; courts construe claims as a matter of law
rubrics_metrics.description: All parts of a claim are considered together; a claim must stand or fall in its entirety and is construed by the court as a question of law (with some factual components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A partial invalidity doctrine does not generally save an indivisible defective claim; interpretive questions about claim meaning are primarily legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for combinations: requisites and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for combinations must separate new and old, be confined to essential elements, and sufficiently describe the union that produces a given effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination claim should explicitly distinguish the novel combination from prior elements, embrace enough elements to produce the claimed result, and cannot be used to claim individual elements unless properly disclosed and claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for an art (process): requisites and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for an art (process) must meet requisites; they cover all ways of practicing the art but cannot simultaneously claim the product in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process claim is proper when the effect results from a new use of natural forces or chemical action, but the claim must be supported by a generic description and cannot improperly claim the product unless supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for machines, manufactures, compositions, and designs — particular requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Different categories (machine, manufacture, composition, design) have distinct requisites (e.g., machine parts covered only in specified connection, chemical composition covers equivalents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine-part claims typically cover the part only in its claimed connection or function; chemical ingredient claims generally cover equivalents; design claims have their own distinct requirements for novelty and ornamentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication and needless repetition of claims improper; disclaimers and amendments governed by delay/fraud rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Needless multiplication or repetition of claims creates ambiguity and is improper. Claims may be disclaimed or amended, but disclaimers/amendments are subject to timing (delay) and fraud constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office and courts discourage superfluous claims and will police multiplicity; disclaimers can cure defects but may be barred by unreasonable delay or evidence of fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of claims for different inventions is improper; inseparable parts and joinder rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not join different inventions; joinder of inseparable parts has special rules and some joinder is allowed for different aspects or uses of the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While claims for different inventions are improper, certain related aspects (e.g., aspects of the same invention or subordinate parts) may be claimed together if they truly form a single inventive unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination doctrine: defined, essential qualities, and inventive skill requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'combination' is an entirety of cooperative elements that produce a new result; it is not a mere aggregation. A combination must produce a new result and be the product of inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essence of a combination is the cooperative law among elements and the new result produced; changes in arrangement, proportions, or elements may produce a new patentable combination if inventive skill is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcombinations and relation to principal combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcombinations and elements relate to the principal combination and have special treatment in claims and reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to subcombinations may be permissible, but whether a subcombination is covered depends on the original disclosure and claim language; reissue can sometimes claim subcombinations consistent with original description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment by sale or other acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment can occur by sale or by other acts that show intent to abandon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions like selling the invention or publicly dedicating it without claiming may constitute abandonment, barring later patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental suggestions and prior abandoned experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments (including abandoned experiments) by others can provide suggestions but are not necessarily prior use bars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of others’ experiments may be relevant to knowledge in the field and to inventor's diligence or obviousness inquiries, but experimental work not publicly accessible typically does not anticipate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogues and acts as evidence of prior use or public knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Catalogues and like publications may be evidence of prior use or knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printed matter, catalogues, and sales literature can serve as prima facie evidence that an invention was known or used prior to the patent date, subject to standard rules of authentication and public availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: purpose, form, secrecy, duration, and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat procedure: purpose and nature; who may file; form and contents; secrecy and duration; proceedings when a subsequent application is filed; caveat cannot be withdrawn; caveat as evidence/estoppel; not assignable; does not bind as to description; belongs to history not description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A caveat gives notice and limited protection while an inventor decides whether to file; it provides rights to notice of later filings during its life, is confidential in some respects, cannot be withdrawn after certain actions, and operates as evidence or estoppel in limited ways. A patent granted without required notice to the caveator may be invalid as to him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of subsequent applications to caveator; scope of caveat protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveator is entitled to notice only of applications filed during the life of the caveat; a patent granted without notice to the caveator can be invalid against him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat protection is time-limited; rights depend on timely filings and required procedural steps—failure by the Patent Office to notify the caveator may have infirmity consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of description is a question of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency of the description may be a question of fact for a jury; the court may also hold a patent void if the description is insufficient on its face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the specification enables one skilled in the art to practice the invention is a factual inquiry, but courts may resolve sufficiency on the face of the specification where plain inadequacy appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture and license issues do not automatically extinguish rights without conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Forfeiture of license may result from breach of condition, but failure to pay money alone is not necessarily a forfeiture; consequences of forfeiture free both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License termination and forfeiture follow contract and equity principles; simple nonpayment is not ipso facto forfeiture unless the agreement so provides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent construed in view of the actual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are construed in view of the actual invention and the nature of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction considers the real nature of the patented subject matter; courts interpret patents in light of the invention's specifics and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result or effect is not patentable; invention is a means not an end
rubrics_metrics.description: A result or effect as such is not patentable; an invention is a means, not an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents must claim concrete means or methods; claiming only an intended result without structure or steps is improper.
